newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: WTO set to create panel in EU grain row.
newsitem.headline: WTO set to create panel in EU grain row.

text.p: A World Trade Organisation (WTO) dispute panel will almost certainly be set up next week to look into a U.S. complaint that European Union grain tariffs violate the body's rules, trade diplomats said on Friday.

They said the United States had renewed a request on March 26 to the WTO's Dispute Settlement Body (DSB) for creation of the panel, which will have six months after its three members are named to come up with a ruling

Under DSB procedures, the request will be granted automatically at the body's April 10 meeting, unless Washington withdraws at the last moment, since it will be the second time U.S. officials will have asked for a panel.
The last request in the long-running dispute on the EU's reference price-based tariff system for wheat, rye, barley, sorghum and rice was filed at a DSB meeting on February 25.
But it was blocked by the EU which said bilateral talks were continuing. WTO rules do not allow countries against whom complaints are filed to block panel requests more than once.

At the last DSB meeting on March 20, the United States did not ask for the case to be included on the agenda -- apparently as a result of EU decisions to implement a new rice import system and a new tariff quota for for U.S. malting barley.
EU farm ministers agreed the barley quota -- allowing import of 30,000 tonnes at 50 per cent of the full duty -- would go into effect in May if Washington dropped its WTO action.

It was not immediately clear why the United States had decided to resurrect the panel request, but trade diplomats said Washington could be aiming to exert pressure to ensure the Brussels concessions were implemented by the end of the month.

The United States first complained to the WTO about the grain tariff system soon after it was introduced in 1995, saying it ran against agreement reached at the end of the 1986-93 Uruguay Round of world trade negotiations.
But until the case re-emerged this year, Washington had twice previously withdrawn or suspended panel requests as bilateral negotiations had appeared to open the way to a settlement.
